meta.title: Who really said "If you’re not part of the solution, you’re part of the precipitate"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Feynman. Quote Investigator traces this chemistry pun to an unattributed 1969 student newspaper; the Feynman credit was invented in a 1999 novel.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you're not part of the solution, you're part of the precipitate'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous chemistry joke, documented from 1969. The Feynman attribution first appears as a scene in a Wes Craven novel.

answer.label: Nobody on record — an anonymous chemistry joke
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ states flatly that “the originator of this quip remains anonymous.” The earliest appearance it located is in The Gateway, the University of Alberta student newspaper, on 12 December 1969, where the line runs across the front-page header with no attribution at all. It circulated for decades as graffiti and as a button slogan before anyone attached a famous name to it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Gateway (University of Alberta), 12 Dec 1969, p. 1

source.excerpt:
if you’re not part of the solution you’re part of the precipitate

— printed across the header of The Gateway, University of Alberta, 12 December 1969, split between the leftmost and rightmost columns, with no attribution.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ concludes that the originator is anonymous, and traces the line from 1969 through student papers, a 1974 newspaper column, 1979 and 1980 sightings, and later literary uses.
The 1969 issue of The Gateway is scanned and readable at the Internet Archive ↗ — the University of Alberta student newspaper for 12 December 1969.

In 1974 the columnist Herb Caen ↗ printed it in the San Francisco Chronicle as a graffito someone had spotted on the UC Santa Cruz science library — still anonymous, five years on, and treated as found writing rather than as anyone’s line.
QI also documents the parent adage, “if you’re not part of the solution you’re part of the problem”, in a separate investigation ↗.
source.excerptNote: The joke is a chemistry pun on the older adage “if you’re not part of the solution, you’re part of the problem”: in chemistry, what does not dissolve into the solution falls out of it as a precipitate.
source.rightsNote: This is an anonymous joke with no identified author and no first publication that can be treated as its origin — its earliest known appearance is an unsigned filler line in a 1969 student newspaper. No copyright status can responsibly be asserted, and it should not be treated as public domain simply because nobody has claimed it.

author.name: Richard Feynman
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Feynman
author.bio: Richard Feynman (1918–1988) shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics and remains the most quotable physicist of his century — a safe-cracking, bongo-playing lecturer with a public reputation for puncturing pomposity. A chemistry pun about not dissolving into the establishment is precisely the kind of thing that reputation attracts. In this case the attraction was literal: a novelist needed a famous physicist to have written on a bunker wall, and picked him.

cite.sourceCitation: Garson O’Toole, “Quip Origin: If You’re Not Part of the Solution You’re Part of the Precipitate,” Quote Investigator, 14 June 2023. Earliest documented appearance: The Gateway (University of Alberta), 12 December 1969, p. 1, unattributed. Earliest Feynman attribution: Wes Craven, Fountain Society: A Novel (1999), ch. 2.

misattribution.heading: Where the Feynman credit came from
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a misattribution, this one has a traceable point of origin — and it is a work of fiction.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ credits no one: “The originator of this quip remains anonymous.” The line was already in print in 1969 and circulating as anonymous graffiti in 1974.

items.scope: The apparent origin of the Feynman credit
items.why: In the horror director’s 1999 novel ↗, a scene set in a New Mexico bunker describes graffiti left by “young physicists who were now household names”, and has Feynman writing this line in the 1960s. The same passage also invents an Einstein graffito. QI’s verdict on it is direct: “QI believes this attribution was invented.”

Wallace put the joke in the mouth of a character in his story “Little Expressionless Animals” (The Paris Review, 1988) — nineteen years after it was already in print. Using a joke is not coining one. Garrison Keillor likewise included it in a 2009 joke book, and it has also been attached to a “Henry J. Tillman”.

misattribution.truthLine: It is an anonymous chemistry joke, in print since 1969. The Feynman credit appears to have been made up for a novel thirty years later — see Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The parent phrase — “if you’re not part of the solution, you’re part of the problem” — was a serious slogan of American activism in the late 1960s. This version is what happens when a science undergraduate hears that slogan and cannot let the double meaning of “solution” go.

That is also why it has no author. It spread the way graffiti and button slogans spread, through campuses and science-fiction conventions, and by the time anyone thought to ask who wrote it the trail was thirty years cold. The famous name arrived last, and arrived from fiction.
context.pull: It spread like graffiti because it was graffiti.
